clue.text: After suspension, wonder about marks received by drunken fighter

indicators.note: what follows is placed after the word for suspension, so that word leads the answer
the word for wonder wraps around the abbreviation for marks
something received is taken inside, so this group goes into the word for drunken

blocks.note: a ban suspends someone from taking part
tight is slang for drunk
awe is a feeling of wonder
M abbreviates marks, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A boxer back from a ban is amazed at the cash a drunken opponent takes home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunken fighter' looks like one phrase, but 'drunken' is wordplay and 'fighter' alone is the definition. 'After suspension' puts the ban first. Marks were Germany's currency before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: A bantamweight is a boxer in one of the lighter weight classes, so a kind of fighter.

clue.text: Look angry as major port sends nothing out east

indicators.note: the round zero is sent away from the port's name and the compass point east is put in its place

blocks.note: Bristol is a large port city in the west of England
O looks like zero, nothing
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Someone glowers as a great harbour loses its eastern trade.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the O in BRISTOL for E and you get BRISTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To bristle is to show anger or indignation, the way an animal's hair stands up when it is hostile.

clue.text: New and splendid singlet, very green

blocks.note: N abbreviates new
A1 means first-rate, with the 1 read as the letter I
a singlet is a sleeveless undershirt, a vest in British usage

explanation.surface: A shopper admires a smart new bright green sleeveless top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very green' looks like a colour; it means inexperienced to the highest degree. A vest is the British word for an undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Green means inexperienced or gullible, so very green is the superlative of naive.

clue.text: Creature’s limb faulty — fuss about it

indicators.note: the word for fuss is placed around the word for faulty, enclosing it

blocks.note: an arm is a limb
ado means fuss or bother
ill can mean bad or faulty, as in ill-made

explanation.surface: An animal's leg is injured and someone makes a fuss about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creature's limb' reads as one phrase about an animal's leg; the creature is the definition and the limb starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An armadillo is an armoured burrowing mammal of the Americas, so it is a creature.

clue.text: Squeeze right through part of plane

indicators.note: the letter passes through the middle of the aircraft part, ending up inside it

blocks.note: a wing is part of an aeroplane
R abbreviates right

explanation.surface: Pushing hard through a narrow gap in an aircraft's structure.
explanation.definitionFit: To wring is to twist and squeeze, as when wringing out wet clothes.

clue.text: He’ll offer cover version finally, one much more likely to go out

indicators.note: only the closing letter of the word before it is used in the build

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
the last letter of version
surer means more certain, far more likely

explanation.surface: A singer's cover version is tipped to be the one that gets released.
explanation.walkthrough: The I has to stand before the N, though the clue names the N first; 'to go out' seems to be surface padding, so treat this parse with some caution.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurer provides insurance cover, protection against loss, in return for premiums.

clue.text: One breaks the law putting cowl on chimney

blocks.note: a cowl is a monk's hood
lum is a Scottish word for chimney

explanation.surface: A lawbreaker caps a chimney with a cowl, the hood-shaped cover on a chimney pot.
explanation.walkthrough: A chimney cowl is a real fitting, which makes the surface sound practical; lum is the Scots chimney, a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoodlum is a thug or gangster, a person who commits crimes.

clue.text: Drink after drink shatters her good faith

indicators.note: something shattered is broken into pieces, so the following words are smashed and reassembled

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: One drink after another wrecks a woman's trust in someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink after drink' reads as heavy drinking; it is a single drink taken the morning after to ease a hangover.
explanation.definitionFit: The hair of the dog is an alcoholic drink taken to cure a hangover caused by earlier drinking.

clue.text: Article I am repeating about singular religious belief

indicators.note: the contracted phrase is used twice, one copy after the other
the second copy goes around the letter for singular

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article
I'm without the apostrophe
the same contraction a second time
S abbreviates singular in grammar

explanation.surface: Someone keeps saying 'I am' about a single faith.
explanation.walkthrough: The contraction is written twice, and only the second copy holds the letter for singular.
explanation.definitionFit: Animism is the belief that spirits dwell in natural objects, places and creatures.

clue.text: Dressed to show the knees, almost — I omit the details

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the phrase loses its final letter

blocks.note: wearing shorts leaves the knees on show

explanation.surface: Someone in shorts with knees on show admits skipping the details.
explanation.walkthrough: IN SHORTS loses its final S.
explanation.definitionFit: In short is said when giving a brief summary and skipping the fuller account.

clue.text: Nerd shows wizard how to do it

blocks.note: to show someone how to do something is to train them; the words how to do it finish this phrase
Harry Potter, the boy wizard

explanation.surface: A geek explains a magic trick to a sorcerer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shows wizard how to do it' reads as one phrase: trains Potter. A trainspotter, someone who logs train numbers, is the British byword for an obsessive nerd.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainspotter is, in British slang, any obsessive enthusiast for trivial detail, a nerd or anorak.

clue.text: One much improved in rubber is to have another walk-over

blocks.note: first meaning: a worn tyre given a new rubber tread
second meaning: to walk over or tread again

explanation.surface: A bridge player who has improved wants another easy win in the rubber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber' and 'walk-over' suggest cards or sport; the first is a tyre, the second a literal second treading.
explanation.definitionFit: A retread is a tyre with a fresh tread moulded on, and to retread is literally to tread a path again.

clue.text: Travel by water with a brutal man

blocks.note: to go is to travel
a rill is a small stream
taken as written

explanation.surface: Taking a boat trip in the company of a thug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Travel by water' looks like one idea, sailing; it splits into travel and water.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorilla is slang for a big, brutish man, especially a hired heavy or bodyguard.

clue.text: Bases host large ships

indicators.note: a host takes a guest in, so the first word holds the next letter inside

blocks.note: feet are the bases of things, as at the foot of a wall
L abbreviates large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Naval bases play host to big vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bases' and 'ships' share a naval picture; bases are feet, and 'large' is just the letter L.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleet is a group of ships sailing or operating together.

clue.text: Guild member’s organ on which many play

indicators.note: to play with letters is to move them about freely

blocks.note: the liver is a body organ
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A guild member's church organ, which many people take turns playing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ on which many play' paints a church organ; the organ is the body's liver. Livery companies are the old trade guilds of the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A liveryman is a full member of one of the City of London's livery companies, the old trade guilds.

clue.text: Reveal Ben may come to like Bede

indicators.note: what the words may come to is a new form, so their letters are rearranged into it

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man called Ben might turn out to resemble the early English monk-historian.
explanation.walkthrough: The Venerable Bede was an eighth-century English monk and historian, and the title is fixed to his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Bede is always called the Venerable Bede, so venerable is the epithet that describes him.

clue.text: Passes — are they at one’s side?

blocks.note: first meaning: passes on, as a parent passes on an heirloom
second meaning, read literally: arms lowered so the hands rest by one's sides

explanation.surface: A question about whether something carried hangs by your side.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is read literally: when your hands are down, they are at your sides. The question mark flags that playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To hand down is to pass something on to the next generation, and hands hanging down rest at your sides.

clue.text: By touring college, finds a sort of family

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all round it, so one word encircles the other

blocks.note: near means by or close to
UCL is University College London

explanation.surface: A visitor touring a college discovers a particular type of household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' looks like a preposition joining the clue together; it is a word in its own right, meaning close.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuclear family is the basic household unit of two parents and their children.

clue.text: Corps eating each starter for breakfast with seconds; there’s no meat course

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so only the opening letter of the meal word is used
the military unit swallows the following letters, holding them inside

blocks.note: the SAS, Special Air Service, is a British army corps
ea is the usual abbreviation for each
the opening letter of breakfast
s abbreviates seconds

explanation.surface: Soldiers tuck into breakfast and go back for second helpings, yet the menu offers no meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' looks like second helpings; it is the abbreviation for seconds of time. SAS swallows EA and B, then S follows: S(EAB)AS S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea bass is a fish, served as the fish course of a meal, which is a course without meat.

clue.text: A month in which we do cleaning

indicators.note: the month abbreviation holds the next word inside it

blocks.note: Sep is the short form of September
taken as written

explanation.surface: Naming the month set aside for spring cleaning.
explanation.walkthrough: The month is in its three-letter calendar abbreviation, and the pronoun goes in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To sweep is to clean a floor with a brush or broom.

clue.text: No end of fuss, in the main, creating poetic structure

indicators.note: no end means the final letter of the next word is removed
the shortened word is placed inside the word for the main

blocks.note: the main is a poetic name for the open sea
to make a stink is to make a fuss

explanation.surface: Endless fuss, out at sea, produces a verse form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' reads as 'mostly'; here the main is the old poetic word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A sestina is a fixed verse form of six six-line stanzas plus an envoi, repeating the same end words.

clue.text: Stare hard at what’s in orbit

blocks.note: first meaning: to look at someone fixedly and aggressively
second meaning: the orbit is the bony socket that holds the eye

explanation.surface: Gazing intently at a satellite circling overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orbit' points to space; it is the eye socket.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball someone is to stare at them, and the eyeball is the organ sitting in the eye socket, called the orbit.

clue.text: Artist offers tea: drop round

indicators.note: the word for drop goes all round the word for tea

blocks.note: to dump is to drop or put down carelessly
cha is a British slang word for tea

explanation.surface: A painter invites someone in for tea: do drop round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop round' reads as a friendly invitation to visit, but it is wordplay. Marcel Duchamp was the French artist behind the urinal 'Fountain'.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Duchamp was a French-American artist central to Dada and conceptual art.

clue.text: Philosopher’s books mount up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible
an alp is a mountain

explanation.surface: A thinker's library of volumes keeps piling higher.
explanation.walkthrough: OT then ALP, read upwards as one string: OTALP reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato was the ancient Greek philosopher, pupil of Socrates and author of the Republic.

clue.text: Particular relaxation inhibits muscle

indicators.note: to inhibit is to hold in check, so one word holds the other within it

blocks.note: rest is relaxation
pec is short for pectoral muscle

explanation.surface: A certain kind of relaxing keeps a muscle from working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Particular' looks like an adjective; here it is a noun, a detail or point.
explanation.definitionFit: A particular is a detail or point, and so is a respect, as in correct in every respect.

clue.text: Wander round about north area in island

indicators.note: the word for wander goes round the next two pieces, enclosing them

blocks.note: to gad about is to wander in search of pleasure
re means about or concerning
N abbreviates north
A abbreviates area

explanation.surface: Roaming the northern part of an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round about' looks like one phrase; 'round' is the container signal and 'about' is a word for concerning. The island is in the Caribbean.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenada is an island nation in the Caribbean, part of the Windward Islands.

clue.text: Armed force’s equipment in terrible shape at the end

indicators.note: the word for equipment is placed inside the word for terrible
only the closing letter of the word before is used

blocks.note: bad means terrible
a rig is a set of equipment
the final letter of shape

explanation.surface: An army's kit ends up in a dreadful state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Armed force's' is read as 'armed force is', and 'shape at the end' means the last letter of shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A brigade is a military unit of several battalions, so an armed force.

clue.text: World’s neatly parcelled out — this divides the country

indicators.note: parcelled out means divided up and redistributed, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The globe is neatly split up, and something splits the land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The country' means the countryside, not a nation. Dry-stone walls, built without mortar, divide fields in upland Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry-stone wall is a mortarless field boundary that divides farmland in the countryside.
